turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I daresay, your sudden concern for Wickham's misfortunes is quite remarkable, considering your previous behavior towards him. I am still waiting to hear how you explain your own actions, rather than merely attempting to shift the blame.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, I find it quite distressing to be lectured on my behavior by someone who has shown so little understanding of propriety and decorum themselves.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured on propriety by someone who has spent years treating those around him with disdain, including those I hold dear.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fail to see how my past behavior towards Wickham is relevant to my feelings for you, Elizabeth. Your own prejudices against me have always been a significant obstacle to our understanding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not interested in hearing your explanations, Mr. Darcy, nor do I wish to be swayed by empty professions of love. You have made it clear, time and again, that you value your own pride and convenience above all else, and I see no reason to believe that has changed.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Elizabeth, that you would so readily dismiss my avowals of love without even considering the possibility that I have genuinely changed, and that my feelings for you are not motivated by pride or convenience.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I find it astonishing that you can be so oblivious to the hurt you have caused me and those I care about, and yet you expect me to believe that your feelings for me are genuine.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am beginning to suspect that your refusal to consider my affections is not entirely due to the reasons you have cited, Elizabeth, but rather a lingering resentment on your part, fueled by your own misconceptions and prejudices.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not the one who has been harboring misconceptions and prejudices, Mr. Darcy. My refusal to consider your affections is not a matter of personal feelings, but a simple recognition of your past actions and the hurt you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find your persistence in clinging to your misconceptions about me to be quite... distressing. It is a failing of your own judgment, rather than any fault of mine, that you continue to misinterpret my actions and intentions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would be surprised at what I consider 'distressing', Mr. Darcy. The fact that you can so callously dismiss the pain you have caused me and others is what truly distresses me.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Elizabeth, that you do not continue to judge me by the actions of my sister, Georgiana, or by your own misconceptions about my character. Your refusal to consider my affections is not only a rejection of me, but also a reflection on your own understanding of what is decent and proper in society.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I think it's rather rich of you to lecture me on what is decent and proper in society, Mr. Darcy, when your own actions have shown you to be woefully lacking in both.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am astonished, Elizabeth, that you would so callously misconstrue the motives behind my behavior, and refuse to acknowledge the sincerity of my affections for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not so foolish as to be swayed by empty professions of affection, Mr. Darcy, when I have seen the damage you have caused to those around you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Elizabeth, that you are mistaken in your assessment of my character. I have acted with the utmost propriety and decorum, and it is you who have been blind to my true nature.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your propriety and decorum are precisely what I find so objectionable, Mr. Darcy. You have consistently shown a lack of empathy and compassion towards those around you, and I will not be swayed by your attempts to present yourself as a paragon of virtue.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I am beginning to tire of your ingratitude and your refusal to acknowledge the esteem in which I hold you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be won over by your condescending tone and empty flattery, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist, Elizabeth, that you reflect upon the circumstances of my life, and consider the difficulties and sacrifices that I have made in order to achieve the position in society that I now hold.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
